question: Why did TikTok take Likeness Detection global and open a public AI checker on 23 November 2026?

rungs.question: Why did TikTok open Likeness Detection to creators and public officials worldwide?
rungs.answer: The sources say the tool lets people find videos that may use their face or likeness without consent and report them for removal. It needs ID verification through a third-party partner and had been tested with US creators since July before this wider release.

evidence.quote: designed to help creators find and remove videos “that may use their likeness without their consent.”
giving them a way to find AI-generated videos that use their face without consent
Likeness Detection has been in testing with US creators since July

counter.text: Digital Music News notes that celebrity deepfake scams "sometimes slip by the appropriate teams and find victims", so the sources describe a reporting tool, not a record of what it has caught. Searched: the three source pages only.

rungs.question: Why does TikTok frame the tool around politicians and public figures?
rungs.answer: RTE, carrying AFP, ties it to European elections next year in Italy, France and Greece, and quotes TikTok's elections lead saying it helps politicians spot AI content shared without consent. The Next Web confirms political accounts are eligible but does not mention elections, so the election reason rests on one site.

evidence.quote: the social media platform seeks to curb AI-generated disinformation ahead of a wave of European elections next year
"Protecting the integrity of the elections is one of the most critical responsibilities that we have at TikTok,"
public figures and political accounts included

counter.text: Digital Music News frames the launch around creators and AI scams aimed at their followers, with no mention of elections. Searched: the three source pages only.

rungs.question: Why can the public checker only say whether a clip was made with TikTok's own tools?
rungs.answer: It does not judge whether content looks artificial. It reads markers that TikTok and its sister apps attach when their AI features are used: C2PA Content Credentials metadata, which can be stripped on download or edit, and an invisible watermark TikTok calls VeraDura.

evidence.quote: the feature is said to zero in on “Content Credentials” metadata and “invisible watermarks”
it looks for the markers TikTok attaches to AI content made with its own tools
but those can be stripped when a clip is downloaded or edited

counter.text: The claim that the watermark survives editing comes from TikTok itself: The Next Web says it is a watermark "which it says is far harder to remove". No source reports an independent test. Searched: the three source pages only.

rungs.mechanism_type: detection model: provenance metadata plus invisible watermark, checked against TikTok/ByteDance tools only

rungs.question: Why does TikTok mark its AI content with these labels at all?
rungs.answer: The sources show TikTok has required creators to label realistic AI content for several years, adopted C2PA in 2024 and says it has labelled over 5 billion AI videos. RTE adds that EU rules since August require deepfakes to be labelled. No source says outright that the EU rule is why TikTok labels.

evidence.quote: TikTok has required content creators to label realistic AI-generated images, audio and video for several years.
including a requirement for deepfakes and other AI-generated content to be labelled
C2PA Content Credentials, an industry standard it adopted in 2024
TikTok says it’s labeled a staggering five billion or so artificial intelligence uploads to date

counter.text: The labelling predates the EU rules that began in August, by RTE's own account, so the rule cannot be the whole reason. Searched: the three source pages only. Why the EU chose a labelling rule, and why TikTok chose labels before it, is not answered in anything read.

rungs.mechanism_type: rule: platform labelling policy alongside EU AI transparency labelling requirement

landing.shows: The ladder shows two different tools resting on one idea: TikTok can vouch for content it marks itself. Likeness Detection relies on ID-verified people reporting matches, and the checker reads only the credentials and watermark TikTok's own apps leave. The election and EU framing comes from one site, and the labelling began before the EU rule.
landing.open_question: When the checker finds no TikTok marker on a clip made with someone else's AI tool, what does that result tell the person who uploaded it?
